passages.title: Family, Media and Peers: What Shapes a Child?
passages.subtitle: How home upbringing and outside forces work together as children grow up
paragraphs: What makes a child grow up to be kind, confident, or rebellious? For generations, people believed that family upbringing was almost the only factor that shaped a young person's character. During the first years of life, parents act as a child's first teacher and primary role model. By watching how parents speak, handle anger, and treat neighbours, young children learn their earliest habits and basic values.

However, once a child starts school, outside forces begin to have a much stronger influence. Friends and classmates—known as peers—quickly become central to a child's world. By the teenage years, many young people care deeply about fitting in with their group. This can lead to peer pressure, which happens when teenagers change their clothes, speech, or behaviour just to be accepted by friends.

Peer pressure is often seen as negative, such as pushing a teenager to skip school or try smoking. Yet psychologists point out that peers can also have a positive effect. For example, a teenager who joins a hard-working study group or a friendly sports team is more likely to improve their grades and stay active.

Another powerful outside factor is daily exposure to media, including television, video games, and social networks. On the positive side, educational TV programmes and science videos can teach children new words, wildlife facts, and respect for other cultures. On the negative side, spending hours watching violent shows or comparing oneself with edited celebrity photos online can increase aggression and lower body confidence.

Because children cannot easily avoid television or smartphones, child psychologists recommend a simple three-step approach for parents to manage media use at home. First, parents should set clear screen limits, such as keeping phones out of bedrooms at night. Next, families should watch key TV shows together so parents can see what their children enjoy. Finally, parents should hold open discussions about advertisements and online content, helping children question whether what they see is realistic.

In short, raising a child is no longer a job done only inside the home. While friends and television certainly shape young minds, research shows that warm and active parents remain the strongest guide. When children feel listened to at home, they are better able to resist harmful peer pressure and make wise choices in the wider world.

passages.title: Elite Sport Funding vs. Grassroots Participation
passages.subtitle: Where should governments spend public money—Olympic medals or everyday fitness?
paragraphs: Every four years, millions of citizens gather around television screens to cheer for their national athletes at the Olympic Games. When a country wins gold medals, celebrations break out across the nation. Behind those victories, however, sits a heated debate about public spending: should governments spend large sums of money supporting a small group of elite athletes, or should they invest in everyday sports for ordinary people?

Supporters of funding elite sport argue that international success brings huge national pride and unites people from different backgrounds. Furthermore, governments invest heavily in talent development—hiring specialist coaches, sports scientists, and doctors—because top athletes act as heroes who inspire children to become active. When a famous swimmer or runner wins a major race, local sports clubs often report a sudden rise in young people signing up to join.

However, health researchers question whether this 'inspiration effect' truly lasts. Surveys taken two years after major international tournaments often show that overall exercise levels among ordinary citizens barely change. Meanwhile, childhood and adult obesity rates continue to climb in many countries, placing heavy pressure on public hospitals. Critics argue that spending millions on a few Olympic stars does little to fix a national health crisis.

Instead, these critics call for greater funding for grassroots participation—everyday community sports open to everyone regardless of age or skill. Building safe cycling paths, free outdoor gyms, and affordable local swimming facilities allows families, elderly people, and beginners to exercise regularly. Even modest amounts of money spent on local parks can benefit thousands of residents every single week.

There is also a debate about how seriously children should take competitive sport. In some talent programmes, children as young as ten train for twenty hours a week in the hope of becoming professionals. While structured training teaches teamwork and discipline, sports doctors warn that pushing young bodies too hard can lead to serious injuries and cause kids to quit sport altogether before they reach adulthood.

Clearly, both elite and grassroots sport have real value. Elite athletes give a country exciting moments to celebrate, while community programmes protect public health. Rather than treating them as enemies, smart governments should ensure that money for elite training never comes at the cost of local parks and school playgrounds—because every future champion begins as a child simply playing for fun.

passages.label: READING PASSAGE 3
passages.instruction: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27-40, which are based on Reading Passage 3 below.
passages.title: Education and Success in Modern Society
passages.subtitle: Is a university degree still the main requirement for a successful life?
paragraphs: For much of the twentieth century, the path to success seemed simple: study hard, earn strong university qualifications, and join a large company for life. A university degree did not just bring a steady income; it also brought high social status and respect from the community. Today, however, many economists and career advisers say this old formula is breaking down.

One reason for this shift is that far more people now attend university than in the past. When only ten percent of young people had a degree, graduates stood out immediately. Now, in many countries, nearly half of young adults graduate from university. As a result, a degree alone no longer guarantees a top job, and some graduates find themselves working in roles that do not require higher education.

At the same time, new routes to success have opened up, especially through entrepreneurship. Thanks to the internet, creative individuals can start an online shop, design mobile apps, or offer digital services with relatively little money. Several famous business founders either left university early or never attended at all, proving that formal certificates are not the only sign of talent.

What, then, are the real requirements for success in modern society? Interviews with business leaders and researchers point repeatedly to personal qualities—especially determination. Starting a business or climbing a career ladder involves frequent setbacks and rejections. People who keep trying, learn from failure, and stay curious often go further than people who have top grades but give up easily.

Another vital requirement is lifelong learning. Because artificial intelligence and automation are changing almost every industry, the skills a person learns at age 21 will not be enough at age 40. Successful workers today regularly update their abilities through short online courses, workplace training, and self-study, regardless of whether they hold a university degree.

Of course, this does not mean university education has lost its value. Doctors, teachers, and scientists still rely on formal degrees, and higher education remains a wonderful way to broaden the mind. Yet modern society is finally recognising a healthier truth: success is not defined by a single piece of paper, but by a person's willingness to keep learning and working hard throughout life.
